questions.question: Why does `TaskQueue.add()` wrap its logic in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` instead of being an `async` function?
options: It's purely a style preference with no functional reason

Because resolve/reject need to be called later, from inside the scheduling/retry logic that runs after add() has already returned — this is the standard pattern for making a callback-driven process awaitable
async functions cannot be used inside classes
new Promise() is required for every function that uses await anywhere in the class
questions.explanation: The task doesn't actually run until a concurrency slot is free, possibly much later — the explicit Promise constructor lets resolve/reject be invoked whenever the job eventually finishes, from deep inside #next()/#runWithRetries().

questions.question: What enforces the concurrency limit in this TaskQueue implementation?
options: A fixed setTimeout delay between tasks
#next() checks #running against #concurrency before starting a new task, and is called again via .finally() each time a running task completes, freeing a slot
JavaScript enforces concurrency limits natively for all async code
questions.explanation: The queue only starts a new task when #running is below the limit; completing a task decrements #running and immediately re-invokes #next() to pull the next pending job, if any.

questions.question: Why are `#pending` and `#running` declared as private class fields instead of regular properties?
options: Private fields are required for a class to extend another class
They encapsulate the queue's internal bookkeeping so external code cannot directly read or corrupt it, the same guarantee closures provided in the module pattern
Private fields make the code run asynchronously
There is no actual difference from public fields
questions.explanation: Private fields (#name) are only accessible within the class body, preventing external code from reaching into and mutating internal queue state directly.

questions.question: In `#runWithRetries`, what happens once `attempt` exceeds `job.retries`?
options: The task silently succeeds with an undefined result
The error is re-thrown, propagating out of #runWithRetries so the task's promise ultimately rejects
The queue retries forever regardless of the retries option
The whole queue stops processing any further tasks
questions.explanation: Once the retry budget is exhausted, the loop re-throws the last error instead of retrying again, which the caller in #next() catches and uses to reject that job's promise.
